I have written research papers in LaTeX for many years.

Over time, I found that the difficult part was not writing an equation such as

$$
\sigma = E\varepsilon.
$$

The real difficulty was managing everything around the manuscript:

- packages,
- personal commands,
- figures,
- references,
- journal styles,
- old papers,
- bibliographic information,
- and the source PDFs behind each citation.

If each new paper begins by rebuilding all of this, scientific writing becomes unnecessarily repetitive.

So I gradually developed a simple rule:

> **The manuscript should change from paper to paper. The writing infrastructure should not.**

My workflow separates the reusable parts of LaTeX from the content of an individual manuscript and connects the bibliography directly to my archive of research papers.

The system itself is simple.

Its value comes from using the same structure consistently over many years.

## A paper should not start from an empty file

When beginning a new journal article, I do not start from an empty LaTeX document and then try to remember which packages, commands, colors, and citation settings I used in the previous paper.

I start from a manuscript template.

A simplified version of my working structure is:

```latex
\documentclass[12pt]{article}

\newcommand{\rootfolder}{D:/Dropbox/Zi}
\newcommand{\graphicfolder}{./figures/}

\input{\rootfolder/zipackage}
\input{\rootfolder/zicommand}

\graphicspath{\graphicfolder}
